claim: The attentional sampling hypothesis suggests that attention rhythmically enhances sensory processing at ~8 Hz when attending to a single object.
source: The attentional sampling hypothesis suggests that attention rhythmically enhances sensory processing when attending to a single (~8 Hz), or multiple (~4 Hz) objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on attentional sampling.

claim: The attentional sampling hypothesis suggests that attention rhythmically enhances sensory processing at ~4 Hz when attending to multiple objects.
source: The attentional sampling hypothesis suggests that attention rhythmically enhances sensory processing when attending to a single (~8 Hz), or multiple (~4 Hz) objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on attentional sampling.

claim: When crossmodally cued toward a conscious image during binocular rivalry, subsequent changes in consciousness occurred at ~8 Hz.
source: When crossmodally cued toward a conscious image, subsequent changes in consciousness occurred at ~8 Hz, consistent with the rates of undivided attentional sampling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When attention was cued toward the suppressed image during binocular rivalry, changes in consciousness slowed to ~3.5 Hz.
source: However, when attention was cued toward the suppressed image, changes in consciousness slowed to ~3.5 Hz, indicating the division of attention away from the conscious visual image.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At attentional sampling frequencies, the strength of inter-trial phase-coherence over fronto-temporal and parieto-occipital regions correlated with changes in perception.
source: In the electroencephalogram, we found that at attentional sampling frequencies, the strength of inter-trial phase-coherence over fronto-temporal and parieto-occipital regions correlated with changes in perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: When cues were not task-relevant, the effects of attentional sampling on perceptual changes disappeared.
source: When cues were not task-relevant, these effects disappeared, confirming that perceptual changes were dependent upon the allocation of attention, and that attention can flexibly sample away from a conscious image in a task-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing attended and non-attended conditions.

claim: Attention can flexibly sample away from a conscious image in a task-dependent manner.
source: When cues were not task-relevant, these effects disappeared, confirming that perceptual changes were dependent upon the allocation of attention, and that attention can flexibly sample away from a conscious image in a task-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing task-dependent effects.

claim: Incoming visual information is periodically enhanced for analysis in the visual system.
source: Recent behavioral and electrophysiological evidence suggests that despite our seamless visual experience, incoming visual information is periodically enhanced for analysis in the visual system (VanRullen, 2016a; VanRullen, 2016b; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Periodic sampling mechanism results from the allocation of visual attention.
source: This periodic sampling mechanism is proposed to result from the allocation of visual attention (Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Dugué et al., 2016; Dugué and VanRullen, 2017a; VanRullen et al., 2007; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alternating windows of high- and low-attentional resources operate to parcel incoming visual information, similar to sequential frames in a video camera.
source: wherein alternating windows of high- and low-attentional resources operate to parcel incoming visual information, similar to the sequential frames that capture film within a video camera (Chakravarthi and Vanrullen, 2012; Vanrullen and Dubois, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The phase or location of the attentional sampling mechanism modulates the accurate detection of a visual stimulus.
source: Whether stimuli are presented at the appropriate phase (Busch et al., 2009; Mathewson et al., 2009; VanRullen et al., 2007) or location (Dugué et al., 2015; Dugué et al., 2016; Dugué and Vanrullen, 2014; Dugué and VanRullen, 2017a; Dugué et al., 2017b; Huang et al., 2015; Landau and Fries, 2012; Song et al., 2014) of this sampling mechanism has been shown to modulate the accurate detection of a visual stimulus
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Target detection depends on the pre-target phase of neural oscillations at approximately 7–8 Hz.
source: To date, primary neural evidence for the rhythmic gating of visual processing stems from the dependence of target detection on the pre-target phase of neural oscillations at approximately 7–8 Hz (Busch et al., 2009; Busch and VanRullen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spontaneous fluctuations in detection may result from the allocation of visual attention toward a single location.
source: These spontaneous fluctuations in detection may result from the allocation of visual attention toward a single location (Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Dugué et al., 2015; Spaak et al., 2014; VanRullen, 2016b; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural excitability cycles gate and filter incoming information for further processing.
source: and support the assumption that neural excitability cycles gate and filter incoming information for further processing (Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; VanRullen, 2013; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spectral analyses applied to high temporal resolution behavioral measures reveal 7–8 Hz modulations in performance following cues to reorient attention.
source: Spectral analyses applied to high temporal resolution behavioral measures reveal 7–8 Hz modulations in performance following cues to reorient attention (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 7-8 Hz modulations in performance slow proportionately when attention is divided between two or more locations.
source: which slow proportionately when attention is divided between two or more locations (e.g. Chen et al., 2017; Holcombe and Chen, 2013; Huang et al., 2015; Landau and Fries, 2012; Landau et al., 2015; VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Following a cue to reorient attention to either the left or right visual hemifield, target detection oscillated at a 4 Hz counterphase rhythm depending on whether cues were congruent or incongruent with the target location.
source: For example, Landau and Fries, 2012 observed that following a cue to reorient attention to either the left or right visual hemifield, target detection oscillated at a 4 Hz counterphase rhythm depending on whether cues were congruent or incongruent with the target location.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Counterphase sampling of visual information persisted at ~4 Hz when attention was directed to two locations on a single object.
source: Critically, this counterphase sampling of visual information persisted at ~4 Hz when attention was directed to two locations on a single object (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Counterphase sampling persisted at ~4 Hz when cues to reorient attention were incongruent with target location.
source: and when cues to reorient attention were incongruent with target location – requiring a subsequent shift in the allocation of attention to a second location (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: An intrinsic ~7–8 Hz attentional rhythm can be allocated over space and time in a sequential manner.
source: These successive fluctuations in target detection and counterphase sampling between locations have led to the suggestion that an intrinsic ~7–8 Hz attentional rhythm can be allocated over space and time in a sequential manner (Dugué et al., 2016; Dugué and VanRullen, 2017a; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Holcombe and Chen, 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; VanRullen, 2013; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During binocular rivalry, incompatible images are presented to each eye which results in stochastic perceptual alternations, with one image visible at a time while the other is suppressed.
source: During binocular rivalry, incompatible images are presented to each eye which results in stochastic perceptual alternations, with one image visible at a time while the other is suppressed (Alais, 2012; Alais and Blake, 2005; Maier et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on binocular rivalry.

claim: Changes in consciousness were occurring rhythmically after the reorientation of attention during binocular rivalry.
source: In an experiment designed to induce or delay these transitions using auditory and tactile cues, we found that changes in consciousness were occurring rhythmically after the reorientation of attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Fluctuations in consciousness occurred at ~8 Hz when the crossmodal cue directed attention toward the dominant visual image.
source: These fluctuations occurred depending on whether the crossmodal cue directed attention toward either the dominant or suppressed visual image, resulting in ~8 Hz and ~3.5 Hz oscillations, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Fluctuations in consciousness occurred at ~3.5 Hz when the crossmodal cue directed attention toward the suppressed visual image.
source: These fluctuations occurred depending on whether the crossmodal cue directed attention toward either the dominant or suppressed visual image, resulting in ~8 Hz and ~3.5 Hz oscillations, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Rhythms at ~8 Hz and ~3.5 Hz were observed in both behavior and the electroencephalogram (EEG).
source: Critically, these rhythms were observed in both behavior and the electroencephalogram (EEG), and were absent when cues were not task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The rhythms at ~8 Hz and ~3.5 Hz were absent when cues were not task-relevant.
source: Critically, these rhythms were observed in both behavior and the electroencephalogram (EEG), and were absent when cues were not task-relevant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The approximate halving of frequency from ~8 Hz to ~3.5 Hz suggests that when non-visual input is inconsistent with the ongoing visual percept, attentional sampling can flexibly orient away from a consciously perceived image.
source: This approximate halving of frequency suggests that when non-visual input is inconsistent with the ongoing visual percept, attentional sampling can flexibly orient away from a consciously perceived image, seemingly 'searching for' alternative sensory information to resolve the conflict.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: 34 subjects participated in the study.
source: Subjects (N = 34) continuously reported the content of their visual consciousness via button press to indicate which image they currently perceived, while neural activity was simultaneously recorded via 64-channel EEG (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Neural activity was simultaneously recorded via 64-channel EEG.
source: Subjects (N = 34) continuously reported the content of their visual consciousness via button press to indicate which image they currently perceived, while neural activity was simultaneously recorded via 64-channel EEG (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study design.

claim: Rivalry stimuli were orthogonal sinusoidal gratings, which underwent sinusoidal contrast modulation, one at 4.5 Hz and the other at 20 Hz.
source: Rivalry stimuli were orthogonal sinusoidal gratings, which underwent sinusoidal contrast modulation, one at 4.5 Hz and the other at 20 Hz (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli, also shown in Figure 1.

claim: In each 3 min block, 12 crossmodal cues were intermittently presented with mean duration 2.6 s.
source: In each 3 min block, we intermittently presented 12 crossmodal cues (mean duration 2.6 s), which were sinusoidally amplitude-modulated signals presented in the auditory and/or tactile modality (auditory, tactile, or combined auditory and tactile) at a frequency congruent with one of the visual stimuli (4.5 or 20 Hz).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Crossmodal cues were sinusoidally amplitude-modulated signals presented in the auditory and/or tactile modality at a frequency congruent with one of the visual stimuli (4.5 or 20 Hz).
source: In each 3 min block, we intermittently presented 12 crossmodal cues (mean duration 2.6 s), which were sinusoidally amplitude-modulated signals presented in the auditory and/or tactile modality (auditory, tactile, or combined auditory and tactile) at a frequency congruent with one of the visual stimuli (4.5 or 20 Hz).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Three null cues (visual-only periods) without any crossmodal stimulation were presented to increase the uncertainty of stimulus timing.
source: To increase uncertainty for the timing of the cues, we inserted three null cues (which we call visual-only periods, Figure 1) without any crossmodal stimulation for a duration of 2.6 s (the average duration of crossmodal cues).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Visual-only periods served as a baseline to compare the behavioral effects of crossmodal cues.
source: The visual-only periods also served as a baseline to compare the behavioral effects of crossmodal cues (see below).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: All cues were separated with uniform jittering by 7–10 s ISI within each block.
source: We randomized the order of all cues, which were separated with uniform jittering by 7–10 s ISI within each block.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: The timing of crossmodal cues was completely independent to perceptual reports.
source: As a result, the timing of crossmodal cues was completely independent to perceptual reports, and cues were presented at any point relative to the onset of the currently dominant percept (i.e., no closed-loop control).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Following the onset of a crossmodal cue, the probability of perceiving a congruent visual image increased only during attended low-frequency cues compared to all other cue types, during the period 0.68 to 3.97 s after cue onset.
source: Following the onset of a crossmodal cue, the probability of perceiving a congruent visual image increased only during attended low-frequency cues compared to all other cue types, during the period 0.68 to 3.97 s after cue onset (repeated measures ANOVAs followed by planned comparisons, FDR q = 0.05, Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: There was no difference in the crossmodal cueing effect when comparing the three types of crossmodal cues (auditory, tactile, and combined auditory tactile).
source: There was no difference in this effect when comparing the three types of crossmodal cues (auditory, tactile, and combined auditory tactile, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the correlation between subjective reports and actual congruent cues, and the perceptual switch index displayed a strong positive correlation (r(32) = 0.46, p = 0.006, two-tailed).
source: The magnitude of these two variables displayed a strong positive correlation (r(32) = 0.46, p = 0.006, two-tailed), suggesting that the cross-modal cueing effect was indeed mediated by attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The cross-modal cueing effect was mediated by attention.
source: The magnitude of these two variables displayed a strong positive correlation (r(32) = 0.46, p = 0.006, two-tailed), suggesting that the cross-modal cueing effect was indeed mediated by attention.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analysis.

claim: When crossmodal cues mismatched with the visual percept at cue onset, the likelihood of switching to the previously suppressed, yet matched visual stimuli significantly increased for attended low-frequency cues compared to all other cue types over a time period from 0.62 to 4.12 s.
source: When crossmodal cues mismatched with the visual percept at cue onset, the likelihood of switching to the previously suppressed, yet matched visual stimuli significantly increased for attended low-frequency cues compared to all other cue types over a time period from 0.62 to 4.12 s (FDR q = 0.05, Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When visual and crossmodal cues matched at cue onset, the effect of attending to low-frequency crossmodal cues delayed changes to the previously suppressed visual percept compared to all other cue types, over the period from 1.05 to 3.58 s.
source: By contrast, when visual and crossmodal cues matched at cue onset, the effect of attending to low-frequency crossmodal cues delayed changes to the previously suppressed visual percept compared to all other cue types, over the period from 1.05 to 3.58 s (FDR q = 0.05, Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Comparison against the visual-only cue period confirmed that the attended low-frequency cues significantly influenced rivalry dynamics, while other cue types did not.
source: Comparison against the visual-only cue period yielded the same conclusion, confirming that the attended low-frequency cues significantly influenced rivalry dynamics, while other cue types did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Compared to visual-only cue periods, first-switches after cue onset occurred earlier for mismatched cues.
source: Compared to visual-only cue periods, first-switches after cue onset occurred earlier for mismatched cues, indicating an earlier change to the congruent, previously suppressed, visual flicker.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cumulative density function data.

claim: Following matched cues first-switches during rivalry were delayed, indicating an extended maintenance of the congruent visual percept when matched with attended low-frequency crossmodal cues.
source: By contrast, following matched cues first-switches during rivalry were delayed, indicating an extended maintenance of the congruent visual percept when matched with attended low-frequency crossmodal cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cumulative density function data.

claim: The facilitation of switches by mismatched cues was observed from 0.63 to 2.45 s and 3.78 to 6.87 s relative to cue onset.
source: The facilitation of switches by mismatched cues was observed from 0.63 to 2.45 s and 3.78 to 6.87 s relative to cue onset, with matched cues delaying switches from 1.27 to 3.77 s after onset (paired samples t-tests, FDR q = 0.05, in Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Matched cues delayed switches from 1.27 to 3.77 s after onset.
source: The facilitation of switches by mismatched cues was observed from 0.63 to 2.45 s and 3.78 to 6.87 s relative to cue onset, with matched cues delaying switches from 1.27 to 3.77 s after onset (paired samples t-tests, FDR q = 0.05, in Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When the temporal frequency of the cue matched the conscious visual flicker at cue onset, the first perceptual switches followed a 7.5–8 Hz rhythm (pcluster < 0.001).
source: Strikingly, when the temporal frequency of the cue matched the conscious visual flicker at cue onset, the first perceptual switches followed a 7.5–8 Hz rhythm (pcluster < 0.001, Figure 3f blue)
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The 7.5-8 Hz rhythm of perceptual switches is consistent with suggestions that attention samples sensory stimulation at a rate of approximately 7–8 Hz.
source: Strikingly, when the temporal frequency of the cue matched the conscious visual flicker at cue onset, the first perceptual switches followed a 7.5–8 Hz rhythm (pcluster < 0.001, Figure 3f blue), consistent with suggestions that attention samples sensory stimulation at a rate of approximately 7–8 Hz (Dugué and VanRullen, 2017a; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim connects the experimental finding to previous literature.

claim: When crossmodal cues were mismatched with the dominant visual image at cue onset, the amplitude spectrum of perceptual switches peaked between 3.3 and 3.75 Hz (pcluster < 0.001).
source: However, when crossmodal cues were mismatched with the dominant visual image at cue onset, the amplitude spectrum of perceptual switches peaked between 3.3 and 3.75 Hz (pcluster < 0.001, Figure 3f magenta).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The 3.3-3.75 Hz rhythm of perceptual changes is consistent with findings that show attention samples two locations at a rate of approximately 3.5–4 Hz.
source: This slower rhythm of perceptual changes is consistent with findings that show attention samples two locations at a rate of approximately 3.5–4 Hz (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; Landau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim connects the experimental finding to previous literature.

claim: No significant peaks were detected for the visual-only condition in the amplitude spectrum of perceptual switches.
source: No significant peaks were detected for the visual-only condition (Figure 3f, gray).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The mismatched cues induced stronger ITPC than the matched cues, at 3.5 Hz over right fronto-central-temporal electrodes [FT8, C6].
source: We found that the mismatched cues induced stronger ITPC than the matched cues, at 3.5 Hz over right fronto-central-temporal electrodes [FT8, C6] (Figure 4a)
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The mismatched cues induced stronger ITPC than the matched cues, at 8 Hz over right parietal-occipital electrodes [P6, PO8].
source: We found that the mismatched cues induced stronger ITPC than the matched cues, at 3.5 Hz over right fronto-central-temporal electrodes [FT8, C6] (Figure 4a) and at 8 Hz over right parietal-occipital electrodes [P6, PO8] (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In right fronto-central-temporal electrodes ([FT8, C6]), 3.5 Hz nITPC and PSI were positively correlated for mismatched cues (r(32) = .38, p = 0.027, two-tailed).
source: In the right fronto-central-temporal electrodes ([FT8, C6]), which significantly differed in 3.5 Hz ITPC based on mismatched or matched percepts (Figure 4a), we found that 3.5 Hz nITPC and PSI were positively correlated for both mismatched (r(32) = .38, p = 0.027, two-tailed, Figure 4c)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In right fronto-central-temporal electrodes ([FT8, C6]), 3.5 Hz nITPC and PSI were positively correlated for matched cue types (r(32) = .34, p = 0.049, two-tailed).
source: In the right fronto-central-temporal electrodes ([FT8, C6]), which significantly differed in 3.5 Hz ITPC based on mismatched or matched percepts (Figure 4a), we found that 3.5 Hz nITPC and PSI were positively correlated for both mismatched (r(32) = .38, p = 0.027, two-tailed, Figure 4c), and matched cue types (r(32) = .34, p = 0.049, two-tailed, Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: For both mismatched and matched cues, increases in 3.5 Hz nITPC facilitated a change in visual consciousness across subjects.
source: Indicating that for both mismatched and matched cues, increases in 3.5 Hz nITPC facilitated a change in visual consciousness across subjects (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation data shown in Figures 4c-d.

claim: In the parieto-occipital electrodes ([P6, PO8]), 8 Hz nITPC was not correlated with the PSI for mismatched cues.
source: In the parieto-occipital electrodes ([P6, PO8]), we found that 8 Hz nITPC was not correlated with the PSI for mismatched cues (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the parieto-occipital electrodes ([P6, PO8]), 8 Hz ITPC was negatively correlated with the PSI during matched cues (r(32) = −0.39, p = 0.023, two-tailed).
source: However, 8 Hz ITPC was negatively correlated with the PSI during matched cues (r(32) = −0.39, p = 0.023, two-tailed, Figure 5c)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Increased 8 Hz nITPC resulted in fewer perceptual switches across subjects during matched cues.
source: However, 8 Hz ITPC was negatively correlated with the PSI during matched cues (r(32) = −0.39, p = 0.023, two-tailed, Figure 5c), demonstrating that increased 8 Hz nITPC resulted in fewer perceptual switches across subjects (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The findings provide novel evidence that attentional sampling exists during binocular rivalry, demonstrated in both behavior and the electroencephalogram (EEG).
source: Our findings provide novel evidence that attentional sampling exists during binocular rivalry, demonstrated in both behavior and the electroencephalogram (EEG).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results.

claim: The study replicated previous evidence that stimulus-driven cues can cause a switch to previously suppressed visual stimuli when mismatched with the current percept.
source: Behaviorally, we replicated previous evidence that stimulus-driven cues can cause a switch to previously suppressed visual stimuli when mismatched with the current percept (to bring about congruence), as well as increase the maintenance of a dominant visual image if cues matched perception (Figure 2; Dieter et al., 2015; Lunghi and Alais, 2015; Lunghi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: Stimulus-driven cues can increase the maintenance of a dominant visual image if cues matched perception.
source: Behaviorally, we replicated previous evidence that stimulus-driven cues can cause a switch to previously suppressed visual stimuli when mismatched with the current percept (to bring about congruence), as well as increase the maintenance of a dominant visual image if cues matched perception (Figure 2; Dieter et al., 2015; Lunghi and Alais, 2015; Lunghi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The ~3.5 Hz rhythm when crossmodal cues were incongruent is consistent with previous reports of divided attentional sampling between two locations.
source: When crossmodal cues were incongruent in temporal frequency with the dominant visual stimulus, switches in visual consciousness occurred earlier, and within a distinct ~3.5 Hz rhythm. This 3.5 Hz rhythm is consistent with previous reports of divided attentional sampling between two locations (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; Landau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim connects the experimental finding to previous literature.

claim: The ~8 Hz rhythm when crossmodal cues were matched is consistent with periodicities in behavioral measures observed when attending to a single visual location.
source: However, when crossmodal cues were matched in temporal frequency to the dominant visual stimulus, changes in visual consciousness demonstrated an ~8 Hz rhythm, consistent with periodicities in behavioral measures observed when attending to a single visual location (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim connects the experimental finding to previous literature.

claim: The ~8 Hz rhythm is consistent with suggestions that a cortical 7–8 Hz attentional rhythm may gate visual processing.
source: However, when crossmodal cues were matched in temporal frequency to the dominant visual stimulus, changes in visual consciousness demonstrated an ~8 Hz rhythm, consistent with periodicities in behavioral measures observed when attending to a single visual location (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013), and suggestions that a cortical 7–8 Hz attentional rhythm may gate visual processing (Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Dugué and VanRullen, 2017a; Fries, 2015).
evidence: This claim connects the experimental finding to previous literature.

claim: Distinct correlates of divided and focused attentional sampling frequencies emerged over right fronto-temporal and right parieto-occipital sites in the EEG.
source: In the EEG (Figures 4 and 5), distinct correlates of these divided and focused attentional sampling frequencies emerged over right fronto-temporal and right parieto-occipital sites, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: ITPC strength at attentional sampling frequencies correlated with the behaviorally reported change in consciousness across subjects.
source: In the EEG (Figures 4 and 5), distinct correlates of these divided and focused attentional sampling frequencies emerged over right fronto-temporal and right parieto-occipital sites, respectively, with ITPC strength at these frequencies correlating with the behaviorally reported change in consciousness across subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Top-down, voluntary attention has been thought to have limited control over perceptual dynamics during binocular rivalry.
source: Traditionally, top-down, voluntary attention has been thought to have limited control over perceptual dynamics during binocular rivalry; attention may alter dominance durations, but cannot halt the process of perceptual reversals entirely (Chong and Blake, 2006; Chong et al., 2005; Chopin and Mamassian, 2010; Dieter et al., 2016b; Dieter et al., 2015; Dieter et al., 2016b; Mitchell et al., 2004; Paffen and Alais, 2011; for bottom-up control, including crossmodal stimulation, see Conrad et al., 2010; Deroy et al., 2014; Guzman-Martinez et al., 2012; Kang and Blake, 2005; Lunghi and Alais, 2013; Lunghi et al., 2010; Lunghi et al., 2014; van Ee et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results clearly show additional dependence on the top-down deployment of attention, as without explicit instruction to attend to crossmodal signals, no facilitatory crossmodal effects emerged.
source: Our results clearly show additional dependence on the top-down deployment of attention, as without explicit instruction to attend to crossmodal signals, no facilitatory crossmodal effects emerged (see also Jack and Hacker, 2014; Talsma et al., 2010; van Ee et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The interaction between low-level stimulus features (temporal frequency) and the allocation of attention indicates the facilitative role of both crossmodal stimuli and attention for perceptual transitions during binocular rivalry.
source: This interaction between low-level stimulus features (temporal frequency) and the allocation of attention indicates the facilitative role of both crossmodal stimuli (Deroy et al., 2014; Deroy et al., 2016) and attention for perceptual transitions during binocular rivalry (Dieter et al., 2016a; Dieter et al., 2015; Dieter and Tadin, 2011; Paffen and Alais, 2011; Zhang et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results supported by citations.

claim: The results are consistent with previous research showing that exogenous feature-based cues can bias rivalry dynamics.
source: Our results are consistent with previous research, which has shown that exogenous feature-based cues can bias rivalry dynamics (Dieter et al., 2015; van Ee et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim connects the experimental findings to previous literature.

claim: The results extend previous reports by revealing an oscillatory basis to changes in visual perception during binocular rivalry.
source: Our results are consistent with previous research, which has shown that exogenous feature-based cues can bias rivalry dynamics (Dieter et al., 2015; van Ee et al., 2009) and extend these reports by revealing an oscillatory basis to these changes in visual perception.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The demonstration of oscillatory changes in visual consciousness evoked by attended crossmodal cues is relevant to current computational models of binocular rivalry.
source: Our demonstration of these oscillatory changes in visual consciousness, which have been evoked by attended crossmodal cues, are also relevant to current computational models of binocular rivalry (e.g. Laing and Chow, 2002; Li et al., 2017; Wilson, 2003).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation connecting the results to computational models.

claim: No current model has accounted for the interaction between attentional allocation and crossmodal stimuli, nor attention as an oscillatory process.
source: No current model has accounted for the interaction we observe between attentional allocation and crossmodal stimuli, nor attention as an oscillatory process.
evidence: This claim is based on review of existing computational models.

claim: Li et al., 2017 described a model for binocular rivalry incorporating attention and mutual inhibition.
source: Most recently, Li et al., 2017 have described a model for binocular rivalry incorporating attention and mutual inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the Li et al. model, attentional modulation is dealt to the sensory representation that has the stronger sensory responses, by providing feedback to monocular-excitatory drives that otherwise increase monotonically with stimulus contrast.
source: In their model, attentional modulation is dealt to the sensory representation that has the stronger sensory responses, by providing feedback to monocular-excitatory drives that otherwise increase monotonically with stimulus contrast.
evidence: This claim describes a previous computational model.

claim: Future models could incorporate an oscillatory increase in excitatory drive as a result of periodic, rather than sustained attentional modulation.
source: Building on our findings, future models could incorporate an oscillatory increase in excitatory drive as a result of periodic, rather than sustained attentional modulation (Fiebelkorn et al., 2018; Helfrich et al., 2018; VanRullen, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: Previous behavioral investigations of attentional sampling have relied upon a brief cue to reorient attention, before estimating the time-course of target detection by densely sampling subject responses over closely spaced target-presentation intervals.

source: For crossmodal stimuli 50 Hz carrier tones were amplitude modulated by 4.5 or 20 Hz sine waves to create digital waveforms, which were either 2, 3.1 or 4 s in duration.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: For tactile stimulation, subjects clasped a wooden ball with their left hand attached to a Clark Synthesis Tactile Sound Transducer (TST429 platinum) housed in a custom sound insulated box.
source: For tactile stimulation, subjects clasped a wooden ball with their left hand attached to a Clark Synthesis Tactile Sound Transducer (TST429 platinum) housed in a custom sound insulated box (Lunghi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental apparatus.

claim: Auditory stimulation was delivered binaurally through Etymotic HD5 noise reduction headphones, with ACCU-Fit foam ear tips to reduce ambient noise.
source: Auditory stimulation was delivered binaurally through Etymotic HD5 noise reduction headphones, with ACCU-Fit foam ear tips to reduce ambient noise.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental apparatus.

claim: Accurate stimulus timing of synchronous visual and crossmodal stimuli was ensured with a WDM-compatible, hardware-independent, low-latency ASIO driver.
source: Accurate stimulus timing of synchronous visual and crossmodal stimuli was ensured with a WDM-compatible, hardware-independent, low-latency ASIO driver (www.asio4all.com), which was necessary to minimize audio buffer duration to sub-millisecond intervals and reduce latency compensation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental methods.

claim: The time-course of stimulus presentation was physically recorded in the EEG for offline analysis.
source: The time-course of stimulus presentation was also physically recorded in the EEG for offline analysis.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Photodiodes were used to record the flicker-envelope of visual stimuli and stored as separate channels in the ongoing EEG.
source: Photodiodes were used to record the flicker-envelope of visual stimuli and stored as separate channels in the ongoing EEG.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental methods.

claim: The waveforms for crossmodal stimulation were simultaneously sent to both the presentation hardware and external electrode channels using a digital splitter.
source: The waveforms for crossmodal stimulation were simultaneously sent to both the presentation hardware and external electrode channels using a digital splitter (Redback A2630 4 Channel Headphone Distribution Amplifier).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental methods.

claim: Stimulus presentation lag was assessed by computing the difference between the recorded frames of trigger-codes and actual physical trace within the EEG as part of data pre-processing.
source: Stimulus presentation lag was assessed by computing the difference between the recorded frames of trigger-codes and actual physical trace within the EEG as part of data pre-processing.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis methods.

claim: The relative timing of behavioral and EEG data was adjusted accordingly as part of the analysis.
source: We adjusted the relative timing of behavioral and EEG data accordingly as part of this analysis.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis methods.

claim: In most cases, no adjustment was necessary, requiring a maximum change of 3 frames in duration on <1% of blocks across all subjects.
source: In most cases, no adjustment was necessary, requiring a maximum change of 3 frames in duration on <1% of blocks across all subjects.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis results.

claim: A maximum of 10 one-minute binocular rivalry blocks were performed prior to experimentation on the first day for all subjects to familiarize subjects with reporting their visual percepts during binocular rivalry.
source: A maximum of 10 one-minute binocular rivalry blocks were performed prior to experimentation on the first day for all subjects. These blocks served to familiarize subjects with reporting their visual percepts during binocular rivalry
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Contrast values for left/right eye, green/red color, and low/high frequency stimulus combinations were adjusted on a logarithmic scale until approximately equivalent total dominance durations were reached (between 1:1 and 1:1.5).
source: Contrast values for left/right eye, green/red color, and low/high frequency stimulus combinations (in total, eight combinations) were adjusted on a logarithmic scale until approximately equivalent total dominance durations were reached (between 1:1 and 1:1.5), with the additional requirement that the average perceptual duration for each stimulus was longer than 1 s.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the calibration procedure.

claim: Prior to experimentation, subjects were tasked with equating the perceptual intensity of tactile and auditory stimulation for each low- and high-frequency condition.
source: Prior to experimentation, subjects were also tasked with equating the perceptual intensity of tactile and auditory stimulation for each low- and high-frequency condition, to achieve approximately equal phenomenological intensity across subjects and stimulus conditions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the calibration procedure.

claim: For all subjects, the amplitude of tactile vibrations was set to the same comfortable, supra-threshold level (approximately equivalent to 65 dB SPL).
source: For all subjects, the amplitude of tactile vibrations was set to the same comfortable, supra-threshold level (approximately equivalent to 65 dB SPL).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: In the absence of visual stimulation, simultaneous auditory and tactile stimuli were presented in a staircase procedure, with subjects adjusting the amplitude of auditory tones to match the perceived intensity of simultaneous tactile vibrations.
source: In the absence of visual stimulation, simultaneous auditory and tactile stimuli were then presented in a staircase procedure, with subjects adjusting the amplitude of auditory tones to match the perceived intensity of simultaneous tactile vibrations.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the calibration procedure.

claim: The calibration procedure for auditory stimuli was performed on each day of testing, to account for differences in the insertion depth of inner-ear headphones across separate days.
source: This calibration procedure was performed on each day of testing, to account for differences in the insertion depth of inner-ear headphones across separate days.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: A total of 24 three-minute binocular rivalry blocks were presented on each of the two separate days of testing.
source: A total of 24 three-minute binocular rivalry blocks were presented on each of the two separate days of testing.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In each block, subjects reported their dominant visual percept during rivalry while receiving occasional crossmodal cues, which were either auditory, tactile, or simultaneous auditory and tactile.
source: In each block, subjects reported their dominant visual percept during rivalry while receiving occasional crossmodal cues, which were either auditory, tactile, or simultaneous auditory and tactile.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: In a given three-minute block, only one of the three types of crossmodal cues was presented.
source: In a given three-minute block, we presented only one of the three types of crossmodal cues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: The order of blocks was randomized for each subject and each day of experimentation.
source: The order of these blocks were randomized for each subject and each day of experimentation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: In each block, 12 trials of crossmodal cues were presented, with each cue being either low (4.5 Hz) or high (20 Hz) frequency auditory and/or tactile stimulation.
source: In each block, 12 trials of crossmodal cues were presented. Each cue was either low (4.5 Hz) or high (20 Hz) frequency auditory and/or tactile stimulation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Six cues were presented for each frequency, with durations composed of three x 2 s, two x 3.1 s, and one x 4 s cues.
source: Six cues were presented for each frequency, with durations composed of three x 2 s, two x 3.1 s, and one x 4 s cues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Over two sessions on separate days, subjects distributed attention between visual rivalry and crossmodal cues based on separate task instructions.
source: Over two sessions on separate days, subjects distributed attention between visual rivalry and crossmodal cues based on separate task instructions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: For their other session, subjects were instructed to focus on reporting their visual percept alone – ignoring any crossmodal cues.
source: For their other session, subjects were instructed to focus on reporting their visual percept alone – ignoring any crossmodal cues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: An additional two practice blocks (3 minutes each) were included during the calibration procedure on the relevant day of experimentation to familiarize subjects with task demands.
source: To familiarize subjects with these task demands, an additional two practice blocks (3 minutes each) were included during the calibration procedure on the relevant day of experimentation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Although 34 subjects were retained for final analysis, five others were recruited and began the experiment, yet failed to complete their second day of experimentation.
source: Although 34 subjects were retained for final analysis, five others were recruited and began the experiment, yet failed to complete their second day of experimentation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about participant attrition.

claim: One subject was removed due to their failure in following task instructions and excessive movement during EEG recording.
source: One other subject was removed due to their failure in following task instructions and excessive movement during EEG recording.
evidence: This is a factual statement about participant exclusion.

claim: At the end of each 3 min block, subjects were asked to verbally report their subjective estimate of the number of crossmodal stimuli which were matched in temporal frequency to the flicker of their dominant visual percept at the point of attended crossmodal cue offset.
source: To evaluate the attentional allocation to both visual and crossmodal stimuli, at the end of each 3 min block we asked subjects to verbally report their subjective estimate of the number of crossmodal stimuli which were matched in temporal frequency to the flicker of their dominant visual percept at the point of attended crossmodal cue offset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The 'attention to cues' index was defined as the correlation coefficient between 24 subjective estimates (one per attended block) and the actual recorded occurrences of congruent stimuli.
source: Then, we defined an index, 'attention to cues' (Figure 2b,x-axis) as the correlation coefficient between 24 subjective estimates (one per attended block) and the actual recorded occurrences of congruent stimuli.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis method.

claim: Button-press data were preprocessed to accurately estimate the timing of changes in visual consciousness during binocular rivalry.
source: We preprocessed the button-press data to accurately estimate the timing of changes in visual consciousness during binocular rivalry.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: Button-presses were categorized as either congruent or incongruent with the ongoing crossmodal stimulus frequency.
source: To analyze the time-course of the probability of a button-press state (Figure 2a), we categorized button-presses (which could correspond to either low- or high-frequency) as either congruent or incongruent with the ongoing crossmodal stimulus frequency.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The probability of a congruent button-press state as a function of time per subject was obtained by averaging responses at each time point across all 144 trials per attention x frequency cue subtype.
source: Then, we obtained the probability of a congruent button-press state as a function of time per subject, by averaging responses at each time point across all 144 trials per attention x frequency cue subtype.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: For visual-only periods, the left button (corresponding to left-eye dominance) was arbitrarily set to congruent prior to the averaging of probability traces within subjects.
source: For visual-only periods, the left button (corresponding to left-eye dominance) was arbitrarily set to congruent prior to the averaging of probability traces within subjects.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: Visual parameters were balanced across all blocks, so the selection of left-eye congruence necessarily balanced across visual frequency and color parameters.
source: As visual parameters were balanced across all blocks, this selection necessarily balanced across visual frequency and color parameters, and we note that the identical analysis performed using right-eye congruence produced equivalent results.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure and its justification.

claim: Mismatched or matched condition comparisons were defined by whether the congruent button (left-eye dominant) was pressed at cue onset.
source: Mismatched (Figure 2c) or matched (Figure 2d) condition comparisons were then defined by whether the congruent button (left-eye dominant) was pressed at cue onset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: In Figure 2c and d, the y-axis for 'Probability of seeing mismatched flicker' reflects the probability of perceptual states that differ in temporal frequency from the crossmodal cue.
source: In Figure 2c and d, we set the y-axis for 'Probability of seeing mismatched flicker', to reflect the probability of perceptual states that differ in temporal frequency from the crossmodal cue.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data presentation.

claim: In Figure 2a,c and d, six conditions were compared with one-way repeated-measures ANOVAs.
source: In Figure 2a,c and d, we compared among six conditions with one-way repeated-measures ANOVAs: 1, visual-only on attend days; 2, visual-only on non-attend days; 3, attended low-frequency; 4, attended high-frequency; 5, unattended low-frequency; and 6, unattended high-frequency.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis.

claim: Significant differences among conditions were defined at those time points that survived corrections for multiple comparisons with planned comparisons between cue types and the visual-only baseline, using FDR at q = 0.05.
source: We defined significant differences among conditions at those time points that survived corrections for multiple comparisons with planned comparisons between cue types and the visual-only baseline, using FDR at q = 0.05 (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: PSI is defined as the difference in the probability of a change in percept when comparing attended low-frequency to four other crossmodal cues.
source: To quantify crossmodal effects during binocular rivalry, we defined the perceptual switch index (PSI). PSI is the difference in the probability of a change in percept when comparing attended low-frequency to four other crossmodal cues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis metric.

claim: For the y-axis in Figure 2b, PSI was calculated as the difference in the probability of viewing a congruent visual flicker over the period 1–4 s after stimulus onset.
source: For the y-axis in Figure 2b, we calculated the PSI as the difference in the probability of viewing a congruent visual flicker over the period 1–4 s after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The same subtraction was used to compare the probability of viewing the previously suppressed visual flicker following mismatched and matched cues, for the period 2–4 s after onset.
source: The same subtraction was used to compare the probability of viewing the previously suppressed visual flicker following mismatched (Figures 4c and 5c) and matched cues (Figures 4d and 5d), for the period 2–4 s after onset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The shorter time window of 2-4 s was selected to capture when the crossmodal effects on binocular rivalry emerged for mismatched and matched cues.
source: This shorter time window was selected to capture when the crossmodal effects on binocular rivalry emerged for mismatched and matched cues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis rationale.

claim: A similar pattern to the results displayed in Figures 4 and 5 was shown when a wider window was used (e.g. 0–4 s).
source: A similar pattern to the results displayed in Figures 4 and 5 was shown when a wider window was used (e.g. 0–4 s, data not shown).
evidence: This is a factual statement about additional analysis results.

claim: For the spectral analysis, the focus was on the first perceptual switches, which were the first time-point recording a change in button-press state after cue onset.
source: For our spectral analysis (Figure 3), we focused on the first perceptual switches, which were the first time-point recording a change in button-press state after cue onset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: To account for individual variation in the amount of overall switches, the proportion of switches at each time point was first calculated at the subject level, before averaging across all subjects.
source: To account for individual variation in the amount of overall switches, the proportion of switches at each time point was first calculated at the subject level, before averaging across all subjects.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: Button-presses were sampled at 60 Hz (or every 16.7 ms).
source: We sampled button-presses at 60 Hz (or every 16.7 ms).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data collection.

claim: For the spectral analysis of perceptual switches, a single-taper fast Fourier transform (FFT) was applied to the period 0.5–2 s after cue onset (Nyquist = 30 Hz, a half bandwidth = 0.67 Hz).
source: For the spectral analysis of perceptual switches (Figure 3f), we applied a single-taper fast Fourier transform (FFT) to the period 0.5–2 s after cue onset (Nyquist = 30 Hz, a half bandwidth = 0.67 Hz).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The 0.5-2 s window was selected to restrict the analysis so that all the analyzed trials occurred during an attended cueing period, and to remove transient button presses occurring early in the cue period.
source: This window was selected to restrict the analysis so that all the analyzed trials occurred during an attended cueing period (as the minimum crossmodal cue duration was 2 s), and to remove transient button presses occurring early in the cue period, which were unlikely to be caused by crossmodal match or mismatch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis rationale.

claim: To assess the statistical significance of behavioral spectra, a two-stage statistical testing procedure was used as applied in previous investigations of attentional sampling and electrophysiological research.
source: To assess the statistical significance of behavioral spectra we used a two-stage statistical testing procedure as applied in previous investigations of attentional sampling (Landau and Fries, 2012) and electrophysiological research (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: At the first stage of statistical testing, significant frequencies were detected (at p < 0.005 uncorrected) through a non-parametric randomization procedure.
source: At the first stage, we first detected significant frequencies (at p < 0.005 uncorrected) through a non-parametric randomization procedure.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: A null distribution of first switches was generated by randomly shifting switch-times within each subject, while keeping the number of perceptual switches the same.
source: In this procedure, after obtaining the spectral amplitude for the observed data across subjects, we generated a null distribution of first switches during the same cue period by randomly shifting switch-times within each subject, while keeping the number of perceptual switches the same.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: 5000 surrogate datasets were generated to test the null hypothesis that there were no temporal effects on the timing of perceptual switches.
source: We generated 5000 surrogate datasets in this way, to test the null hypothesis that there were no temporal effects on the timing of perceptual switches.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: The spectral amplitude at a certain frequency was regarded as significantly above chance if the observed spectral amplitude exceeded the top 99.5% of the null-distribution of amplitudes at each frequency generated by surrogate data.
source: We regarded the spectral amplitude at a certain frequency to be significantly above chance, if the observed spectral amplitude exceeded the top 99.5% of the null-distribution of amplitudes at each frequency generated by surrogate data.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: At the second stage, a cluster criterion was applied, which corrects for multiple comparisons across multiple frequencies through a permutation procedure.
source: At the second stage, we applied a cluster criterion, which corrects for multiple comparisons across multiple frequencies through a permutation procedure (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: The first-level significance (p<0.005 uncorrected) was required to be sustained for at least two neighboring frequencies.
source: We required that the first-level significance (p<0.005 uncorrected) be sustained for at least two neighboring frequencies, and retained the sum of their clustered test-statistics (amplitudes in this case) as our observed data.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: Candidate clusters survived the second order analysis when their observed cluster-based test-statistics exceeded the top 95% of the null distribution, or corrected to pcluster <0.05 if testing across multiple clusters.
source: Candidate clusters survived this second order analysis when their observed cluster-based test-statistics exceeded the top 95% of the null distribution, or corrected to pcluster <0.05 if testing across multiple clusters.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: EEG was recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz using three BrainAmp amplifiers and 64-channel ActiCap, with the impedance of each electrode kept below 10 kΩ.
source: EEG was recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz using three BrainAmp amplifiers and 64-channel ActiCap (BrainProducts; RRID:SCR_009443), with the impedance of each electrode kept below 10 kΩ.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the EEG recording procedure.

claim: Ground and reference electrodes were AFz and FCz at recording, respectively.
source: Ground and reference electrodes were AFz and FCz at recording, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the EEG recording procedure.

claim: After re-referencing the data to the average of all channels, linear detrending and bandpass filtering (0.1–60 Hz with a Hamming-windowed finite impulse response filter) were performed and the data was down-sampled to 250 Hz before time-frequency analysis.
source: After re-referencing the data to the average of all channels, we performed linear detrending and bandpass filtering (0.1–60 Hz with a Hamming-windowed finite impulse response filter) and down-sampled the data to 250 Hz before time-frequency analysis.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the EEG data preprocessing.

claim: All time-frequency analyses were performed using the Chronux toolbox and custom MATLAB scripts.
source: We performed all time-frequency analyses using the Chronux toolbox ((http://chronux.org; Bokil et al., 2010); RRID:SCR_005547), and custom MATLAB scripts.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis tools.

claim: To resolve the frequencies of interest (especially between 3.5 and 4.5 Hz), a single-taper Fourier transform with a time-window of 2 s was used, which resulted in a half bandwidth (W) of 0.5 Hz.
source: To resolve our frequencies of interest (especially between 3.5 and 4.5 Hz), we used a single-taper Fourier transform with a time-window of 2 s, which resulted in a half bandwidth (W) of 0.5 Hz (W = 1/2).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The half bandwidth of 0.5 Hz is capable of resolving differences between 3.5 and 4.5 Hz, as demonstrated in Figures 4b and 5b.
source: This half bandwidth is consequently capable of resolving differences between 3.5 and 4.5 Hz, as demonstrated in Figures 4b and 5b.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis capability.

claim: To assess the neural correlates of attentional sampling, the inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) within electrodes was analyzed over multiple time-frequency points.
source: To assess the neural correlates of attentional sampling (Figures 4 and 5), we analyzed the inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) within electrodes, over multiple time-frequency points (Bastos and Schoffelen, 2015).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: ITPC is an amplitude-normalized measure of the degree to which EEG responses are phase-locked to the onset of an exogenous cue, ranging between 0 (random phase over trials) and 1 (perfect phase consistency over trials).
source: ITPC is an amplitude-normalized measure of the degree to which EEG responses are phase-locked to the onset of an exogenous cue, ranging between 0 (random phase over trials) and 1 (perfect phase consistency over trials).
evidence: This is a factual statement defining the ITPC metric.

claim: Due to the stochastic nature of perceptual alternations during binocular rivalry, the number of available trials for analysis in each mismatched and matched cue type ranged from 12 to 36 trials across subjects.
source: Due to the stochastic nature of perceptual alternations during binocular rivalry, the number of available trials for analysis in each mismatched and matched cue type ranged from 12 to 36 trials across subjects (after averaging first across subjects, the mean number of trials was 24 (±1.5) trials across matched/mismatched and attention conditions).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data characteristics.

claim: To equate the number of mismatched and matched cue types for the analysis, the minimum number of trials recorded for a given cue combination was identified across subjects, and subjects with greater numbers of trials had their observed number of trials supplemented by downsampling with replacement.
source: Because the bias level (or expected chance level for pure noise data) of ITPC is strongly influenced by the number of trials, we took additional measures to equate the number of mismatched and matched cue types for the analysis. To achieve this aim, the minimum number of trials recorded for a given cue combination was identified across subjects. Following this, subjects with greater numbers of trials had their observed number of trials supplemented by downsampling with replacement from their recorded trials, equating them to the predefined minimum for each condition.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The ITPC was computed on the resampled dataset, and this process was repeated 100 times.
source: Upon this resampled dataset, the ITPC was computed, and this process repeated 100 times.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: The difference in ITPC between auditory, tactile, and combined auditory and tactile cues was not significant, so crossmodal cue types were combined within each subject.
source: As the difference in ITPC between auditory, tactile, and combined auditory and tactile cues was not significant, we proceeded by combining crossmodal cue types within each subject.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis results and procedure.

claim: To investigate the neural correlates of attentional sampling, evoked ITPC was analyzed, which is the increase in ITPC during 0 to 2 s after onset compared to −2 to 0 s before onset.
source: To investigate the neural correlates of attentional sampling, we analysed evoked ITPC, the increase in ITPC during 0 to 2 s after onset compared to −2 to 0 s before onset.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis procedure.

claim: A two-stage statistical testing procedure was used for the ITPC analysis, similar to the behavioral spectral analysis.
source: Similar to our statistical approach for the behavioral spectral analysis described above, we used a two-stage statistical testing procedure for this analysis.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: At the first stage, a t-test (two-tailed) was performed comparing whether evoked 3.5 and 8 Hz ITPC differed between mismatched and matched conditions across subjects at each electrode.
source: At the first stage, we performed a t-test (two-tailed) comparing whether evoked 3.5 and 8 Hz ITPC differed between mismatched and matched conditions across subjects at each electrode.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: At each electrode, the mean evoked ITPC value obtained from the downsampling method was used.
source: At each electrode, we used the mean evoked ITPC value obtained from the downsampling method described above.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: If a cluster of at least two neighboring electrodes with the same t-score polarity at p < 0.05 (uncorrected) was found, where inter-electrode distance did not exceed 3.5 cm, the analysis proceeded to the second stage of statistics.
source: As a result of the t-tests, if we found a cluster of at least two neighboring electrodes with the same t-score polarity at p < 0.05 (uncorrected), where inter-electrode distance did not exceed 3.5 cm, we proceeded using this cluster in the second stage of statistics.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: As a result of the cluster criterion, a minimum size of 2-electrode clusters was always identified.
source: As a result of this cluster criterion, we always identified a minimum size of 2-electrode clusters (Figures 4a and 5a).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis results.

claim: At the second stage, the absolute value of the sum of observed t-scores within the identified cluster was computed and retained as the observed test-statistic.
source: At the second stage, we first computed the absolute value of the sum of observed t-scores within the identified cluster, which we retained as our observed test-statistic (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: To create the null distribution, condition labels (mismatch and match) were randomly shuffled for each electrode within each subject, to create two surrogate datasets the same size as the original mismatch and match conditions.
source: To create the null distribution, condition labels (mismatch and match) were randomly shuffled for each electrode within each subject, to create two surrogate datasets the same size as our original mismatch and match conditions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: The t-scores were computed for each electrode based on surrogate datasets, and the electrode with the maximum t-score and the maximum t-score of its neighbors were retained.
source: Then the t-scores were computed for each electrode based on our surrogate datasets, and the electrode with the maximum t-score and the maximum t-score of its neighbors retained.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: The sum of t-scores was retained per shuffle, and this procedure was repeated 2000 times to obtain a null distribution of the sum of t-scores around the maximum electrode for each shuffle of the surrogate data.
source: The sum of these t-scores were then retained per shuffle, and this procedure repeated 2000 times to obtain a null distribution of the sum of t-scores around the maximum electrode for each shuffle of our surrogate data.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: When the observed sum of t-scores was within the top 5% (or cluster corrected to p < 0.05), it was concluded that there was a significant difference between mismatch and match conditions.
source: Against this distribution, the sum of observed t-scores for the candidate cluster was then compared. When the observed sum of t-scores was within the top 5% (or cluster corrected to p < 0.05) then we concluded that there was a significant difference between mismatch and match conditions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: The raw data in this study are available via the Monash University Figshare repository.
source: The raw data in this study are available via the Monash University Figshare repository (https://figshare.com/projects/Crossmodal_binocular_rivalry_attention_sampling_project/56252).
evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability.

claim: Analysis code is available via GitHub.
